title: refactor: share a single pad kernel between lpad and rpad
body:
## Which issue does this PR close?

- Closes #26303.

## Rationale for this change

lpad and rpad had four copies of the same per-row padding loop, plus two copies of the scalar fast path. The only real difference between them was whether the fill gets written before or after the string.

## What changes are included in this PR?

- New `unicode/pad.rs` with a single kernel, generic over a `PadSide` trait (`LeftPad` / `RightPad`, same idea as `LeftRightSlicer` in `common.rs`). `lpad.rs` and `rpad.rs` are now thin wrappers with just the docs and tests.
- The no-fill case goes through the same loop with `" "` as the fill, so the second loop is gone.
- `parse_target_len` replaces the six copies of the `i32::MAX` / negative length check. Error text is unchanged.

Two things came out of benchmarking:
- Once the shared length check had its error branch inline, it stopped getting inlined into the hot loop and the no-fill path got noticeably slower. Moving the error into a `#[cold]` function fixed that.
- The non-ASCII path now writes the fill in whole copies instead of one char at a time with a `%` per char. That's where the speedup below comes from.

I also added `no fill` cases to the pad benchmarks (first commit). None of the existing cases covered a 2-arg call with a length column, which is the path this changes the most.

## What is the testing strategy for this PR?

Existing lpad/rpad unit tests and sqllogictests pass unchanged. I added tests in `pad.rs` that pass array arguments to both functions, since most of the existing ones go through the scalar fast path: no fill, fill, nulls, zero length, truncation, string view input, a partial multi-char unicode fill (`rpad('josé', 6, 'ñéx')`), and the too-large length error.

## Benchmarks

`cargo bench -p datafusion-functions --features unicode_expressions --bench unicode_expressions -- "pad size="`, main vs this branch, run back to back on the same machine:

- non-ASCII string with a fill (8 cases): 31–48% faster
- everything else (40 cases): somewhere between −16% and +14% in both directions, which is about the noise on my machine. The scalar cases, whose logic didn't change, moved by the same amount.

Happy to re-run anything if someone wants different numbers.

## Are there any user-facing changes?

No.

---

Separately, I found that a negative length coming from a column panics on main (`pad_data_capacity` does `len as usize`). That's not part of this PR, and I'll open its own issue.

title: fix: avoid quadratic row-buffer accounting in sort merges
body:
## Which issue does this PR close?

Follow-up to #25372, related to #23174.

## Rationale for this change

Multi-key sorts over many small batches spend quadratic time accounting for retained row buffers, delaying their first merged output.

The merge caches one encoded row buffer per input stream. Each new batch currently scans every cache slot to recalculate the reservation. Reading the first batch from each of N streams therefore requires N full scans. A large merge can spend seconds doing this bookkeeping in a single Tokio poll.

## What changes are included in this PR?

- Track each stream's reserved bytes and update the total by that stream's change, making each accounting update constant-time.
- Keep the existing charge while a buffer is reused. Failed buffer growth and stream completion release only that stream's charge.
- Add a SQL benchmark that sorts two million rows loaded in 32-row batches. Two sort keys exercise the affected row-format merge. Data generation happens before timing.

## What is the testing strategy for this PR?

A focused regression test fills a bounded memory pool, then rejects growth of a reused row buffer. It checks that the failed stream releases its previous reservation while another stream remains accounted for.

The SQL benchmark runs a single query, with no concurrent workload:

```bash
cargo run --release --bin benchmark_runner -- sort_small_batches --iterations 5
```

With four Tokio workers and one partition, nine executions per version in interleaved groups gave:

| Single-query wall time | `upstream/main` | This PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| Median | 4.82 s | 1.30 s |
| Range | 4.52–5.64 s | 1.23–1.46 s |

That is about **3.7× faster**. Both optimized builds use the same upstream base and return all two million rows.

## Are there any user-facing changes?

Large row-format merges perform less bookkeeping while preserving their memory reservations. The SQL benchmark is listed in the benchmark guide, and the internal reservation invariant is documented alongside the per-stream sizes.

Developed with AI assistance.

title: feat: let `SpillCompression::Zstd` carry a compression level
body:
## Which issue does this PR close?

- Related to #16367.

## Rationale for this change

Allows for configuring the zstd compression level for spill files instead of always using arrow's default compression level (3). Possible now that arrow-rs exposes `IpcWriteOptions::try_with_compression_level`.

## What changes are included in this PR?

- `SpillCompression::Zstd` becomes `SpillCompression::Zstd(u32)` with `SpillCompression::DEFAULT_ZSTD_LEVEL = 3`.
- `datafusion.execution.spill_compression` accepts `zstd(<level>)` with a level in 0..=22, parsed and validated at `SET` time. Plain `zstd` means level 3 to preserve current behavior.
- The compression level is passed onto arrow via `IpcWriteOptions::try_with_compression_level`.

## What is the testing strategy for this PR?

- 2 new parse tests in `datafusion/common/src/config.rs`.
- 1 new test in `datafusion/physical-plan/src/spill/mod.rs` to assert that setting zstd compression level actually changes compression behavior.
- sqllogictests in `datafusion/sqllogictest/test_files/information_schema.slt`.

## Are there any user-facing changes?

Yes, breaking change because `SpillCompression` is a public enum. Added an upgrade guide to `docs/source/library-user-guide/upgrading/56.0.0.md`.

title: Window referencing a named window with an added frame, OVER (w ROWS ...), silently drops PARTITION BY and ORDER BY
body:
### Describe the bug

A window that references a named window and adds a frame, such as `OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN ...)`, keeps the frame but silently drops the named window's `PARTITION BY` and `ORDER BY`. The function then runs over all rows as one partition, so values leak across partitions. There is no error.

`OVER w` works. Only the form with the name inside the parentheses is affected.

### To Reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(ticker VARCHAR, ts INT, price DOUBLE) AS VALUES
  ('BTC', 1, 100.0), ('BTC', 2, 105.0), ('BTC', 3, 102.0),
  ('DOGE', 1, 0.1), ('DOGE', 2, 0.2), ('DOGE', 3, 0.15);

SELECT ticker, ts, price,
  MAX(price) OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS named_plus_frame,
  MAX(price) OVER (PARTITION BY ticker ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS inline
FROM t
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY ticker ORDER BY ts)
ORDER BY ticker, ts;
```

```
+--------+----+-------+------------------+--------+
| ticker | ts | price | named_plus_frame | inline |
+--------+----+-------+------------------+--------+
| BTC    | 1  | 100.0 | 100.0            | 100.0  |
| BTC    | 2  | 105.0 | 105.0            | 105.0  |
| BTC    | 3  | 102.0 | 105.0            | 105.0  |
| DOGE   | 1  | 0.1   | 102.0            | 0.1    |
| DOGE   | 2  | 0.2   | 0.2              | 0.2    |
| DOGE   | 3  | 0.15  | 0.2              | 0.2    |
+--------+----+-------+------------------+--------+
```

The first DOGE row gets BTC's price (102.0).

### Expected behavior

`OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN ...)` should inherit `w`'s `PARTITION BY` and `ORDER BY` and add the frame, as in the SQL standard and PostgreSQL, so both columns above match. Per the standard (and PostgreSQL), it should be an error if the referencing window also specifies `PARTITION BY`, specifies `ORDER BY` when `w` already has one, or if `w` itself has a frame.

### Additional context

`match_window_definitions` in `datafusion/sql/src/select.rs` only rewrites `WindowType::NamedWindow` (`OVER w`). For `OVER (w ...)`, sqlparser produces a `WindowType::WindowSpec` with `window_name = Some(w)`, and `window_name` is never read when planning, so `w` is dropped. A `WINDOW w2 AS (w1 ...)` definition that references another window likely has the same problem.

Reproduced with datafusion-cli ; the same code path is unchanged on main.

title: Piecewise merge join: semi/anti joins fail with an internal error on RunEndEncoded keys
body:
### Describe the bug

With `datafusion.optimizer.enable_piecewise_merge_join = true`, every existence join that `PiecewiseMergeJoinExec` plans (`LeftSemi`, `LeftAnti`, `RightSemi`, `RightAnti`, so `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` with a range predicate) fails when the join key is `RunEndEncoded`:

```
Internal error: Min/Max accumulator not implemented for type RunEndEncoded(non-null Int32, Int32).
```

The same queries return the right rows with the flag off, and PWMJ's classic joins (`INNER` / `LEFT` / `RIGHT` / `FULL`) return the right rows on the same REE tables.

### To Reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE l AS SELECT column1 AS id, arrow_cast(column2, 'RunEndEncoded("run_ends": non-null Int32, "values": Int32)') AS v
FROM (VALUES (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, NULL), (4, 5));
CREATE TABLE r AS SELECT column1 AS rid, arrow_cast(column2, 'RunEndEncoded("run_ends": non-null Int32, "values": Int32)') AS v
FROM (VALUES (20, 2), (21, NULL), (22, 6));

SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_piecewise_merge_join = true;

-- LeftSemi / LeftAnti
SELECT id FROM l WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM r WHERE l.v < r.v);
SELECT id FROM l WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM r WHERE l.v < r.v);
-- RightSemi / RightAnti
SELECT r.rid FROM l RIGHT SEMI JOIN r ON l.v < r.v;
SELECT r.rid FROM l RIGHT ANTI JOIN r ON l.v < r.v;
```

All four fail with the internal error above. The plan is `PiecewiseMergeJoin: operator=Lt, join_type=LeftSemi, ...` (resp. `RightSemi`, ...).

### Expected behavior

The rows the flag-off plan returns:

| query | expected |
|---|---|
| `EXISTS` | 1, 2, 4 |
| `NOT EXISTS` | 3 |
| `RIGHT SEMI` | 20, 22 |
| `RIGHT ANTI` | 21 |


### Additional context

The existence paths reduce a batch of keys to a single extreme key in `extreme_key` (`joins/piecewise_merge_join/existence_join.rs`), used by the left existence stream and by the right existence buffered fold in `exec.rs`. For non-nested keys it calls `min_batch` / `max_batch` from `datafusion-functions-aggregate-common`, which have no `RunEndEncoded` arm. Classic joins never take the extreme, which is why they are unaffected.

#26247 / #26248 report the same error message for `MIN`/`MAX` aggregates, but that fix is in `get_min_max_result_type`: the planner casts REE to its value type before the accumulator runs. PWMJ calls the kernels directly on the evaluated join keys, so it does not go through that coercion and #26248 does not fix this.

### Willingness to contribute

None

title: Validate Parquet INT96 timezone values when configuration is assigned
body:
# related PR

Related: apache/datafusion#17498. Follow-up to PR #25628; independently actionable.

## Problem

`datafusion.execution.parquet.coerce_int96_tz` is an unchecked optional string.
Invalid timezone text can enter configuration, then fail during Parquet schema
inference or scan setup rather than at the offending SET/table option.

A regression should demonstrate early rejection of:

```sql
SET datafusion.execution.parquet.coerce_int96_tz = 'Not/A_Timezone';
```

Current behavior is established by code inspection, not an executed SQL repro.
No panic is claimed: the current timezone parser returns a configuration error.

## Evidence / root cause

- `datafusion/common/src/config.rs:1422`: `Option<String>` field.
- `datafusion/datasource-parquet/src/source.rs:542`:
  `parse_coerce_int96_tz_string` parses Arrow's `Tz` at consumption time.
- `datafusion/datasource-parquet/src/file_format.rs`: schema inference calls the
  same helper.
- `datafusion/common/src/config.rs:2074`: existing `ConfigTimeZone` (added for
  `execution.time_zone`, #25788) wraps a private string, validates with the same
  Arrow `Tz` parse, preserves input spelling, and already has a parse-before-
  assign `ConfigField for Option<ConfigTimeZone>`.
- Both protobuf decoder families currently transport the timezone as a string.

The timezone syntax invariant is owned by consumers rather than configuration.

## Why it matters

Invalid settings can remain latent until a Parquet operation uses them. Once
PR #25628 lands, the nearby INT96-unit option validates at assignment, leaving inconsistent behavior
between related options and repeated late parsing.

## Invariant / desired behavior

A stored timezone is absent or accepted by the timezone parser used by the
Parquet reader. Failed updates preserve prior state, including None. Reset
restores absence.

Validation is unconditional at assignment, but application stays conditional:
without `coerce_int96`, a valid configured timezone still has no effect.
`coerce_int96 = None` must remain distinct from an explicit nanosecond unit.

Preserve timestamp unit, timezone spelling/metadata, and actual read values.

## Proposed direction

Reuse `ConfigTimeZone`: it and `parse_coerce_int96_tz_string` both accept
exactly what `s.parse::<arrow::array::timezone::Tz>()` accepts, so the accepted
language is unchanged. Only the error message differs (it mentions UTC offsets,
which are in fact accepted). Do not add another timezone wrapper.

Change the field to a validated optional timezone. Adapt consumers to obtain an
`Arc<str>` from the validated text without repeating syntax validation. Remove
the old parser once no callers remain. Keep runtime checks concerning actual
file/schema compatibility; they are not syntax validation.

## Scope

### In

- Session SET/reset, direct configuration APIs, and table-format options.
- Schema-inference and explicit-schema scan paths.
- Both protobuf decoders/encoders and affected FFI option transport.
- Docs and migration examples for public Rust field assignments.

### Out

- Changes to session timezone coercion, daylight-saving interpretation,
  timezone normalization, accepted timezone language, or INT96 conversion math.
- Applying this timezone when INT96 coercion is disabled.
- Broad timezone framework refactors or changes to unrelated string configs.

## Compatibility / risks

This intentionally rejects invalid text even while coercion is disabled; today
such text can remain unused. Document the earlier error as a user-visible change.

A typed public field is a Rust source break: use `api change` and add a migration
example such as `Some("UTC".parse()?)`. Preserve protobuf string fields/numbers.
Valid legacy messages must decode; invalid serialized timezones must return
errors, including when no INT96 unit is configured.

Do not assume the helper's IANA wording defines its full accepted language:
verify UTC-offset forms accepted by Arrow. Preserve case sensitivity and original
spelling rather than introducing normalization.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Invalid timezone SET/table options fail immediately, with or without a unit.
- [ ] Invalid updates preserve Some/None state; reset restores None.
- [ ] Valid accepted timezone forms retain existing semantics and spelling.
- [ ] Both protobuf decoders reject malformed timezone strings.
- [ ] Valid/absent timezone and unit combinations round-trip.
- [ ] No unit means no timezone application; explicit units still apply it.
- [ ] Inferred and explicit-schema reads retain expected unit, metadata, values.
- [ ] Consumers no longer parse configuration timezone syntax late.
- [ ] Migration and error-timing changes are documented.

## Tests / verification

- Unit tests: UTC, an IANA zone, offset forms supported by the current parser,
  invalid/empty input, failed replacement/unset update, nested keys, and reset.
- SQLLogicTests: SET/SHOW/error/unchanged state/reset; invalid table options with
  inferred and explicit schemas using an existing Parquet fixture.
- INT96 read tests: configured timezone with unit absent, explicit nanoseconds,
  and microseconds. Assert output field types/timezone and values, not just success.
- Protobuf tests for both conversion families: valid/absent round-trips and
  invalid input independent of whether a unit is present.
- Check affected FFI config round-trips and builds without Parquet to avoid
  accidentally making a general configuration type feature-dependent.
- Run targeted config/protobuf/INT96/SLT tests, then repository-required
  formatting, lint, and extended validation. No runtime speedup is claimed.

title: Refactor `HashJoinExec` by splitting regular/existence join into dedicated streams

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem or challenge?

Part of
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/26225

See issue for general background, below is HJ-specific rationales.

Hash Join operator has accumulated certain complexity, it's easier to proceed with future feature/improvements after a refactor.

Specifically, when we want to add spilling, or existence join fast path
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/24768

 Then regular joins and existence joins have sufficiently different optimization opportunities, or implementation logic, so that splitting them is simpler than reusing the same state machine.



### Describe the solution you'd like

Incremental rewrite HJ into 2 dedicated paths
1. https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/26227
2. Implement the existence join path

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

### Additional context

In the existing implementation:
- NLJ and HJ: reused execution state machine for existence and regular join. NLJ has implemented spilling and some existence join fast path, I think that causes unnecessary complexity -- lots of local flag are used to route the execution for different join logic
- SMJ: already split due to the same concern

### Willingness to contribute

None

title: PoC: Explicit Invariant Regions in the Physical Optimizer
body:
## Which issue does this PR close?

<!--
We generally require a GitHub issue to be filed for all bug fixes and enhancements and this helps us generate change logs for our releases. You can link an issue to this PR using the GitHub syntax. For example `Closes #123` indicates that this PR will close issue #123.
-->

- Closes #.

## Rationale for this change

<!--
 Why are you proposing this change? If this is already explained clearly in the issue then this section is not needed.
 Explaining clearly why changes are proposed helps reviewers understand your changes and offer better suggestions for fixes.  

Please explain the problem you are trying to solve in terms of the user-visible
behavior, rather than the implementation.

For example, "The code in `foo.rs` doesn't handle nulls" is a symptom of the
implementation. "COUNT(DISTINCT) returns wrong results when the column contains
nulls" is the user-visible problem.
-->

The default physical optimizer pipeline works for the optimizations implemented in DataFusion core. However, there are many hidden assumptions between optimizer rules that make the pipeline work as a whole (e.g., rule A must run before rule B to produce a valid plan).

These implicit constraints make extensions harder, whether adding new rules within DataFusion core or implementing custom pipelines downstream.

This PR introduces **explicit invariant regions** to make these hidden constraints visible and verifiable, making the optimizer easier to understand, extend, and maintain.

Note that this PR does not introduce new constraints. I think of this primarily as a **"removing uncertainty"** step. The assumptions already exist; this PR provides a mechanism to surface them so that:

1. Developers can understand the expectations between optimizer rules.
2. We can automatically test whether rules preserve those expectations.
3. Extensions can make more informed decisions about where to insert or rearrange rules.

The tradeoff is a certain learning curve for this mechanism. After prototyping the idea, I feel that once we become familiar with the concept, it can make long-term maintenance easier. However, it definitely looks confusing at first glance, and I'm still thinking about how to improve this part.

(Note: The implementation is currently underdocumented; most of the ideas are explained in this writeup.)

### Two Types of Constraints

This section explains two types of constraints, with one example each. The following figure illustrates two invariant regions in an example optimizer pipeline, which will be explained further below.

```text
                           Invariant Regions
Rule List                   Aggr              Req
--------------------------------------------------------
InitialPhysicalPlanner
                            +-- BEGIN
...                         |
LimitedDistinctAggregation  |
...                         |
                            +-- END
EnsureRequirements
                                              +-- BEGIN
...                                           |
                                              +-- END
ExtensionRule1                                (inactive)
ExtensionRule2                                (inactive)
EnsureRequirements                            (restore)
                                              +-- BEGIN
...                                           |
SanityCheckPlan                               |
                                              +-- END
```

- **Region 1, CanonicalAggregatePlan (Aggr):** Maintains canonical aggregation shapes in this region, the rules inside this region can kept simpler by only handling the canonical aggregate shape
- **Region 2, InputRequirementsSatisfied (Req):** Ensures execution requirements remain satisfied. The example demonstrated temporary turning off/on in the middle to make extension easier.

### Type I: Optimization-Coverage Constraints (Soft)

#### Progressive refinement in the optimizer pipeline

The default optimizer pipeline is a progressive refinement process, where the possible plan shapes vary across stages.

For example:

- At rule 1, a hash join might have only one canonical representation.
- At rule 20, the same logical join might have five possible physical representations.

A rule that rewrites joins could be much simpler when placed at an earlier stage.

Requiring every rule to handle every possible representation, regardless of its position, can unnecessarily bloat the implementation of earlier rules.

#### Making soft constraints explicit

Built-in rules already rely on such canonicalization assumptions, allowing them to match only canonical plan shapes and keep their implementations simple.

Soft constraints provide a mechanism to make these assumptions explicit and verifiable, so custom optimizer pipelines can either:

- Follow the constraints to preserve the same optimization coverage. (Another interpretation is that these constraints help extension rules find suitable positions in the pipeline.)
- Opt out of the constraints, accepting the possibility of losing optimization coverage from built-in rules.

#### Example: LimitedDistinctAggregation

See https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/26069 for a concrete example of how relying on a canonical aggregation shape can simplify an optimizer rule.

The corresponding invariant region would be:

```text
CanonicalAggregatePlan
- Established: After InitialPhysicalPlanner
- Ends: After LimitedDistinctAggregation
```

This is illustrated as Region 1 (Aggr) in the figure above.

### Type II: Execution-Validity Constraints (Hard)

These constraints are required for correct execution. Extensions must preserve them to ensure that plans remain runnable.

#### Example: EnsureRequirements

Consider a partitioned hash join.

Before enforcing requirements:

```text
HashJoinExec(mode=Partitioned, on=[t1.k = t2.k])
  Scan(t1)  <-- Not hash-partitioned on t1.k
  Scan(t2)  <-- Not hash-partitioned on t2.k
```

The plan represents the intended computation, but its children do not satisfy the hash join's distribution requirements.

After `EnsureRequirements`:

```text
HashJoinExec(mode=Partitioned, on=[t1.k = t2.k])
  RepartitionExec(hash(t1.k), N)
    Scan(t1)
  RepartitionExec(hash(t2.k), N)
    Scan(t2)
```

Now the join's distribution requirements are satisfied.

We can express this as an invariant region, as shown in the figure above.

Within this region, every optimizer rule must preserve the invariant. If a rule violates it, the checker reports the failure immediately after that rule (when validation is enabled).

For extensions, the responsibility is explicitly one of the following:

1. Preserve the existing ordering/distribution guarantees.
2. If a transformation breaks those guarantees, repair the plan internally.
3. Alternatively, explicitly leave the region, perform transformations without those guarantees, and restore them before reentering. (demonstrated in the figure above)




## What changes are included in this PR?

<!--
There is no need to duplicate the description in the issue here, but it is sometimes worth providing a summary of the individual changes in this PR.
-->
1. Add a configuration option, `validate_optimizer_invariants`, to control invariant checking. Use a feature flag to enable validation in tests/CI while skipping it in release builds.
2. The main change is in `physical-optimizer/src/optimizer.rs`, introducing invariant regions into the existing optimizer rule list.

The PoC implements the following regions, which are not exactly the same as the examples above:

- **NoEmbeddedProjection:** Soft constraint for projection shape canonicalization.
- **HashJoinModeResolved:** Soft constraint for hash join mode resolution.
- **InputRequirementsSatisfied:** Hard constraint; see the example above.

One thing that remains implicit is **which optimizer rules establish the invariants**.

For example, in the figure above, the canonical aggregation region is established by initial physical planning, while the `InputRequirementsSatisfied` region is established by `EnsureRequirements`.

Therefore, downstream custom optimizer pipelines must follow the same assumptions and manually declare these regions after the corresponding rules have established their invariants.

## What is the testing strategy for this PR?

<!--
We typically require tests for all PRs in order to:
1. Prevent the code from being accidentally broken by subsequent changes
2. Serve as another way to document the expected behavior of the code

Briefly describe how this PR is tested, and point to the specific tests you added. For example: 'This new feature is covered by the `sqllogictest` cases added in `foo.slt`'.

If this PR does not add tests, explain why. For example, if the change is already covered by existing tests, please mention it.

You should also check the `codecov` bot reply on this PR to confirm the changed code is exercised.
-->

## Are there any user-facing changes?

<!--
If there are user-facing changes then we may require documentation to be updated before approving the PR.

If there are any breaking changes to public APIs, please add the `api change` label.
-->

title: Show nullability of an explicit CastExpr target in its display
body:
## Which issue does this PR close?

- Closes #26358.

## Rationale for this change

A cast to an explicit target field can change only the nullability of its input. `UnionExec` adds one to align its inputs. `CastExpr` displayed only the data type, so EXPLAIN showed a same-type cast such as `CAST(1 AS Int64)` with no visible effect.

## What changes are included in this PR?

- `CastExpr`'s `Display` appends `;N`, the notation schemas already use, when the cast has an explicit target field that is nullable.
- Casts built from a bare type and `fmt_sql` are unchanged.
- Updated plan expectations. The only change in each is the added `;N`.

## What is the testing strategy for this PR?

- New unit test `test_display_explicit_target_nullability` in `cast.rs`.
- Existing sqllogictest, insta and pruning predicate expectations updated.

## Are there any user-facing changes?

Physical plan text in EXPLAIN changes for these casts. No API changes.

title: Physical CastExpr display hides nullability changes, so union coercion casts look like no-ops
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem or challenge?

`UnionExec` aligns its inputs to the merged union schema. When an input differs only in nullability, it wraps that input in a `ProjectionExec` of `CastExpr::new_with_target_field`, which keeps the data type and changes only the field's nullability.

`CastExpr`'s `Display` prints only the data type, so in EXPLAIN this cast looks like a no-op:

```
ProjectionExec: expr=[..., CAST(trf_id@11 AS Int32) as trf_id, ...]
```

`trf_id` is already `Int32`. The only thing this cast does is make the column nullable, because another union input is nullable. Nothing in the plan says that, so a reader has to go back to the source code to see why the cast exists. We hit this when we changed one table's column from nullable to `NOT NULL`. A new same-type cast showed up in every plan that unions that table with a nullable input.

The same thing happens in DataFusion's own plans, for example in `cte.slt`:

```
ProjectionExec: expr=[CAST(1 AS Int64) as id]
```

### Describe the solution you'd like

When the cast has an explicit target field that is nullable, print the nullability the way schemas already do, with `;N`:

```
ProjectionExec: expr=[CAST(1 AS Int64;N) as id]
```

Casts built from a bare type (`CastExpr::new`) are unchanged. Their nullability follows the input, so there is nothing extra to show. `fmt_sql` is also unchanged.

I have a small patch ready. It updates goldens in 6 slt files, 1 insta snapshot and the pruning predicate unit tests. In every one of them the only change is the added `;N`.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- Rely on `datafusion.explain.show_schema`. That shows the projection's output schema, but it is verbose and off by default. It also doesn't tie the nullability to the cast that changed it.
- Print `;N` only when the nullability actually changes. `Display` has no access to the input schema, so it can't tell.
- Use a different notation, for example `CAST(a AS Int32 NULL)`. `;N` matches the existing schema display, but I'm happy to change it.

### Additional context

The patch also shows a case that was hard to see before. `rewrite_expr_to_prunable` rebuilds a plain `CAST(col AS T)` as `CastExpr::new_with_target_field(.., cast.target_field(), None)`. For a plain cast, `target_field()` is a placeholder nullable field. So the rewrite turns a cast whose nullability follows its input into one that is always nullable, and it drops the original cast options (`None`). This is harmless for pruning, since statistics columns are nullable anyway. It is visible now as `CAST(c1_min@0 AS Int64;N)` in the pruning predicate display.

title: perf: add a GroupsAccumulator for array_agg(DISTINCT)
body:
## Which issue does this PR close?

- Closes #26347.

## Rationale for this change

`array_agg(DISTINCT x)` had no `GroupsAccumulator`. Grouped queries fell back to `GroupsAccumulatorAdapter`, which keeps one `DistinctArrayAggAccumulator` per group, each with its own hash table and encoded rows. With many groups this dominates memory and CPU.

## What changes are included in this PR?

New `DistinctArrayAggGroupsAccumulator`:

* Each distinct value is encoded once with a `RowConverter` into a `Rows` buffer shared by all groups, so a value that appears in many groups is stored once.
* Groups record `(group_index, value_index)` pairs, deduplicated in one hash set.
* `evaluate` builds the `ListArray` with a counting sort by group.
* It also covers `array_agg(DISTINCT x ORDER BY x)`, sorting each group by the encoded rows.
* `EmitTo::First` drops values only referenced by emitted groups.

Small refactors: the DISTINCT / ORDER BY check is shared by the row and groups paths (`distinct_sort_options`), and the one-row-per-list `convert_to_state` is shared with `ArrayAggGroupsAccumulator`.

`state_compat` now compares list results as multisets for DISTINCT without ORDER BY, since the element order is not defined there. The row accumulator returns hash table order.

## Are these changes tested?

* **Unit tests** cover dedup across batches, nulls with and without IGNORE NULLS, FILTER, ORDER BY DESC, `EmitTo::First`, state/merge, `convert_to_state`, dictionary types, and a differential check against `DistinctArrayAggAccumulator`.
* **`state_compat`** passes with the new accumulator included.
* **`array_agg.slt`** gains grouped cases mixing DISTINCT with `count(*)`, FILTER, ORDER BY and IGNORE NULLS. The existing aggregate slt files pass.

## Benchmarks

Measured locally with a criterion benchmark (not included here, happy to add it): one 8192-row Utf8 batch, `update_batch` plus `evaluate`, the new accumulator against `GroupsAccumulatorAdapter` over `DistinctArrayAggAccumulator`. Apple M-series:

| groups | input | groups accumulator | adapter (before) | speedup |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| 100 | ~25 distinct | 154 µs | 251 µs | 1.6x |
| 100 | ~7800 distinct | 384 µs | 969 µs | 2.5x |
| 1000 | ~25 distinct | 173 µs | 1.42 ms | 8.2x |
| 1000 | ~7800 distinct | 382 µs | 2.26 ms | 5.9x |
| 8192 | ~25 distinct | 279 µs | 10.2 ms | 36x |
| 8192 | ~7800 distinct | 414 µs | 10.4 ms | 25x |

Live heap after `update_batch`, measured with a counting global allocator: 65 536 Utf8 rows in 8 batches. `size()` tracks these within ~10% for both.

| groups | input | groups accumulator | adapter (before) |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| 100 | ~25 distinct | 11 KB | 720 KB |
| 1000 | ~7800 distinct | 2.2 MB | 9.9 MB |
| 8192 | ~25 distinct | 1.7 MB | 18.3 MB |
| 65536 | ~7800 distinct | 2.2 MB | 100.7 MB |

Memory now grows with the number of distinct values instead of the number of groups.

## Are there any user-facing changes?

No API changes. `array_agg(DISTINCT x)` without ORDER BY may return elements in a different (still unspecified) order.

title: fix: keep EliminateGroupByConstant from requalifying group expressions
body:
## Which issue does this PR close?

No issue filed. The reproduction is below.

## Rationale for this change

`EliminateGroupByConstant` re-plans the original group expressions over the new `Aggregate` with `LogicalPlanBuilder::project`. Column normalization falls back to the input schema of the aggregate. Thus an unqualified group expression, such as an extracted leaf `__datafusion_extracted_1`, becomes `m.__datafusion_extracted_1` when the input is a `SubqueryAlias: m`. The new aggregate does not output that name, and the rule fails:

```
Optimizer rule 'eliminate_group_by_constant' failed
caused by
Schema error: No field named m.__datafusion_extracted_1.
```

The input plan is valid, and the rule turns it into an invalid one. We reach it when we optimize a plan, bind its parameters with `replace_params_with_values`, and optimize again. The bound value makes a group key redundant only after `ExtractLeafExpressions` has rewritten the plan. In a single `optimize` call, `EliminateGroupByConstant` runs before `ExtractLeafExpressions` in each pass, so I could not reproduce it there. Since #26184, the arguments of filtered aggregates no longer go into a common-expression projection between the aggregate and the alias, so the aggregate can sit directly on the alias and the problem shows.

```rust
let ctx = SessionContext::new();
ctx.sql("CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT * FROM (VALUES (TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01T00:00:00', named_struct('a', 'x'), 1)) AS v(ts, s, x)")
    .await?.collect().await?;
let scan = ctx.table("t").await?.into_unoptimized_plan();
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::from(scan)
    .alias("m")?
    .aggregate(
        vec![
            date_bin(
                cast(placeholder("$1"), DataType::Interval(IntervalUnit::MonthDayNano)),
                col("ts"),
                lit(ScalarValue::TimestampNanosecond(Some(0), None)),
            ),
            get_field(col("s"), "a").alias("c"),
            col("ts"),
        ],
        vec![
            sum(col("x") + lit(1)).filter(col("x").gt(lit(0))).build()?,
            max(col("x") + lit(1)).filter(col("x").lt(lit(5))).build()?,
        ],
    )?
    .build()?;
let state = ctx.state();
let plan = state.optimize(&plan)?;
let plan = plan.replace_params_with_values(&ParamValues::List(vec![
    ScalarValue::Utf8(Some("1 minute".into())).into(),
]))?;
state.optimize(&plan)?; // fails with the error above
```

## What changes are included in this PR?

- The rule builds the projection with `Projection::try_new` and does not re-plan the group expressions. A kept key or an aggregate becomes a column of the schema of the new aggregate. A redundant key keeps its expression, which reads only bare GROUP BY columns that the new aggregate outputs unchanged. An item gets an alias only when its name differs from the original output field, so existing plans do not change.
- The rule leaves an aggregate with a `GroupingSet` unchanged, because its output fields do not map one to one to `group_expr`.

## What is the testing strategy for this PR?

- New unit test `test_eliminate_with_unqualified_reference_to_qualified_input`. It fails without the change, with the same schema error.
- `cargo test -p datafusion-optimizer` and `cargo test -p datafusion-sqllogictest --test sqllogictests` pass. No existing plan changes.

## Are there any user-facing changes?

No API changes. A plan that failed in this rule now optimizes.

title: perf: resolve parquet leaf columns in O(1) during statistics collection
body:
## Which issue does this PR close?

- Part of #21968.

This revives #21987 by @adriangb, which was closed while stale and never reviewed. The two commits are his, rebased onto current `main`. The fix was never carried into #22829 or #22830, and the quadratic lookup is still on `main`.

## Rationale for this change

Planning a query against a wide-schema Parquet table takes time quadratic in the number of columns, even when the query reads only one or two of them.

`DFParquetMetadata::statistics_from_parquet_metadata` resolves every field in the logical file schema to a Parquet leaf column. Both branches resolve each field with an O(N) lookup:

- When the file has statistics, it calls `StatisticsConverter::try_new`. That does a linear `Schema::column_with_name`, then calls `parquet_column`, which does a linear `Fields::find` and a linear scan for the first leaf under the matched root.
- When the file has no statistics, it calls `parquet_column` directly.

This happens once per field, so the cost is O(N²) per file, on every query plan, for every file in the table.

## What changes are included in this PR?

- A new crate-private `LeafResolver` (`datafusion/datasource-parquet/src/leaf_resolver.rs`). It builds two maps once per file: Arrow field name to root index, and Parquet root index to first leaf index. Both call sites use it in place of the per-field linear lookups, which makes the statistics pass O(N) per file.
- `LeafResolver` gives the same results as `parquet_column`, including its tie-breaks: the first Arrow field with a given name wins, and the lowest leaf index for a root wins. When a leaf exists, it builds the converter with `StatisticsConverter::from_column_index`, which yields the same converter `try_new` would (same leaf index, same Arrow field, same physical type).
- A field with no Parquet leaf (a nested type, or a name missing from the file schema) falls back to `StatisticsConverter::try_new`. This reproduces its exact error for an unknown column, and it is needed because `from_column_index` cannot express "this column has no Parquet leaf".
- The `parquet_metadata_statistics` benchmark now also covers 1024 columns, because the quadratic term only shows up past a few hundred columns.

Rebasing onto `main` conflicted in `statistics_from_parquet_metadata`. The resolution keeps every change made on `main` since #21987, including the omitted-null-count handling and the untrusted min/max order checks, and changes only how each field's converter is built.

**Known limitation:** schemas with many nested fields still take the O(N) fallback for those fields. apache/arrow-rs#9882 proposes a constructor that takes an `Option<usize>` leaf, which would remove the fallback. Flat wide schemas never take it.

## What is the testing strategy for this PR?

- Six unit tests in `leaf_resolver.rs`. The main one is a differential test: for every field name in a schema that mixes primitives, a nested struct, a nested list, duplicate field names and absent names, `LeafResolver::leaf_index` must return exactly what `parquet_column` returns. The tie-break rules are the risky part: getting either backwards would silently attribute one column's statistics to another, and nothing in the existing suite covers duplicate names. The other tests cover:
  - nested and missing names resolving to no leaf
  - converters built through the resolver matching `try_new`
  - byte-identical error text for an unknown column
  - an empty schema
- Existing suites: `-p datafusion-datasource-parquet --lib`, `-p datafusion --test parquet_integration`, and the `parquet_statistics`, `listing_table_statistics`, `parquet_sorted_statistics` and `parquet_nested_schema_pruning` sqllogictest files.

### Benchmarks

`wide_schema` (1024 vs 8 columns × 256 files), run locally on an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D. These are Criterion medians, `main` (e732212ca) against this branch:

| Query | main | this PR | change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Q01 wide | 694.5 ms | 522.9 ms | −24.7% |
| Q02 wide | 528.0 ms | 350.3 ms | −33.7% |
| Q03 wide | 529.2 ms | 353.4 ms | −33.2% |
| Q04 wide | 617.2 ms | 445.5 ms | −27.8% |
| Q01–Q04 narrow | — | — | within ±0.5% |

For every wide query the confidence intervals do not overlap. The two sides ran one after the other on the same machine, not interleaved.

## Are there any user-facing changes?

No. `LeafResolver` is crate-private and the statistics produced are unchanged. Planning against wide-schema Parquet tables is faster.

---

title: Memory limit test `smj_with_mem_limit_1` is flaky
body:
### Describe the bug

`memory_limit::memory_limit_validation::smj_mem_validation::smj_with_mem_limit_1`, added in #23988 and first released in 55.1.0, fails intermittently on 32-vCPU Linux hosts. In the failures the measured RSS growth is about 200 MB, well above the 160 MB allowance (`40_000_000 * 4`). Across repeated runs the result is bimodal: it either fits under the allowance or lands near 200 MB.

The test leaves little headroom even where it passes. On an Apple Silicon Mac it measures 149.4–149.8 MB against the 152.6 MiB allowance in five out of five runs, a margin of about 2%.

### To Reproduce

On a 32-vCPU x86_64 Linux host (we see it on Amazon Linux 2023, EC2 c7a.8xlarge):

```sh
git checkout 55.1.0
cargo test --profile ci -p datafusion --features extended_tests --test core_integration -- \
  memory_limit::memory_limit_validation::smj_mem_validation::smj_with_mem_limit_1_runner
```

The failure is intermittent, so repeat the run several times.

Example failure output:

```
Memory before: 140.9 MB, Memory after: 340.9 MB
Query: SELECT sum(rr.v) FROM generate_series(0, 0) AS l(k) JOIN (SELECT i % 1 AS k, i AS v FROM generate_series(1, 5000000) AS r(i)) rr ON l.k = rr.k, Memory usage: 200.0 MB, Memory limit: 152.6 MB

thread 'memory_limit::memory_limit_validation::smj_mem_validation::smj_with_mem_limit_1' panicked at datafusion/core/tests/memory_limit/memory_limit_validation/utils.rs:286:5:
Memory usage exceeded the theoretical limit. Actual: 200.0 MB, Expected limit: 152.6 MB
```

Measured usage in three failing runs: 197.8 MB, 199.7 MB, 200.0 MB. Four other runs of the same suite passed. 

### Expected behavior

The test passes deterministically on supported CI hosts, or its allowance leaves enough headroom for allocator variance between platforms.

### Additional context

- **Spilling is not the problem.** The assertion that `SortMergeJoinExec` spilled passes in the failing runs, and `smj_with_mem_limit_2` and `smj_no_mem_limit` pass.
- **The baseline is much higher on Linux.** The baseline query peaks at about 141 MB of RSS on the Linux host, against about 62 MB on macOS. The jump of roughly 50 MB between passing and failing runs suggests glibc malloc retaining an extra arena heap, which is 64 MB on 64-bit. We have not verified this, for example with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX`.
- **Our measurement helper was modified.** We patch `measure_max_rss` in `utils.rs` to refresh only the current PID instead of calling `System::new_all()` inside the monitor task, and to seed the peak with a reading taken before the query. In our environment the full refresh could take long enough that the short baseline query finished before any sample, leaving the baseline RSS at 0 and turning the "delta" into absolute RSS. This may deserve a separate issue, and we can open a PR if that's useful.

Possible fixes:

- raise the allowance for `smj_with_mem_limit_1`, for example to `40_000_000 * 5`;
- base the allowance on the spill metrics rather than a fixed RSS factor;
- run the memory-validation subprocesses with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` set, if the arena explanation holds.

title: feat: add `SessionConfig::update_extension` so libraries can share one `ProtoDecoderRegistry`
body:
## Which issue does this PR close?

- Follow-up to https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/24631. No separate issue.

## Rationale for this change

A session carries one `ProtoDecoderRegistry`, as a `SessionConfig` extension. Today the only way to attach it is `SessionConfig::with_extension`, which **replaces** the extension. If two libraries each register extension decoders, the second one silently discards the decoders of the first one. The failure shows only later, at decode time, as "No decoder is registered".

We found this when we moved datafusion-distributed to the registry API. Distributed registers its plans in the worker `SessionConfig`, then gives the config to the user's session builder. A user who attaches their own registry there removes the distributed decoders.

```rust
// Before: library B discards library A's decoders
config = config.with_extension(Arc::new(registry_a));
config = config.with_extension(Arc::new(registry_b));
```

## What changes are included in this PR?

A new generic method, `SessionConfig::update_extension`. It changes an extension in place, and creates it with `Default` if it is not there. If another config shares the extension, it is cloned first (`Arc::make_mut`), so that config does not change.

```rust
// After: each library adds to the same registry, in any order
config.update_extension(|registry: &mut ProtoDecoderRegistry| {
    register_execution_plan::<MyExec>(registry)
})?;
```

The method is generic because `datafusion-execution` does not depend on `datafusion-proto-models`, where the registry is defined. It is useful for any extension that more than one part of an application writes to.

The docs for `ProtoDecoderRegistry` and `register_execution_plan`, and the unreleased 56.0.0 upgrade guide, now recommend `update_extension` and say not to use `with_extension` for the registry.

## What is the testing strategy for this PR?

- `proto::registry::tests::libraries_add_to_one_session_registry`: two "libraries" register different plans through `update_extension`. Both names stay registered. A config cloned between the two calls keeps only the first name.
- A doc test on `update_extension`.

## Are there any user-facing changes?

Yes, one new public method on `SessionConfig`. It is additive and does not break anything. No behavior changes for existing callers of `with_extension`.

title: fix: handle aggregate name collisions from casts
body:
## Which issue does this PR close?

Closes #26221.

## Rationale for this change

`sum(x)` and `sum(CAST(x AS FLOAT))` get the same schema name, so using both in one query fails even with separate aliases. The collision happens in the aggregate node before the projection applies those aliases.

## What changes are included in this PR?

Use the display name for colliding aggregates when it differs from their schema name. Expression rebasing then resolves the original expression to the renamed aggregate column.

This keeps the naming change local to SQL aggregation. Queries without distinct output aliases still get the existing duplicate projection name error.

## What is the testing strategy for this PR?

SQLLogicTest cases cover both argument orders, multiple casts, `TRY_CAST`, `COUNT`, grouping, `HAVING`, and `ORDER BY`. The existing `approx_distinct` regression now checks successful execution, and an `EXPLAIN` case checks the aggregate names.

## Are there any user-facing changes?

Queries that aggregate a column and a cast of it can now plan successfully when their output names are distinct.

AI assistance: Claude Code generated the patch and tests; Codex read the diff and prepared this description. The scope assumes the fix belongs in SQL aggregate naming rather than changing cast schema names globally.

title: Optimize inner joins with a proven single constant row into Filter/Projection
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem or challenge?

An inner join whose other input is provably one row of literals can remain a `NestedLoopJoinExec`, even though substituting those literals into the join predicate would turn it into a filter and projection.

Besides the join overhead, this loses useful ordering information: `NestedLoopJoinExec` declares that it preserves neither input's order. For an input already ordered by grouping keys, this can prevent downstream aggregation from using that ordering for early emission and state release. A filter/projection can preserve the relevant ordering.

#### Reproducer

Executed with the official `datafusion-cli 52.3.0`:

```sql
SET datafusion.execution.target_partitions = 1;

CREATE TABLE events AS
SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('a', 10), ('a', 30), ('b', 20), ('b', NULL))
AS v(account_id, event_time);

EXPLAIN FORMAT INDENT
SELECT e.account_id, e.event_time, b.cutoff
FROM (SELECT 25 AS cutoff) b
JOIN events e ON e.event_time < b.cutoff;
```

Actual physical plan:

```text
ProjectionExec: expr=[account_id@1 as account_id, event_time@2 as event_time, cutoff@0 as cutoff]
  NestedLoopJoinExec: join_type=Inner, filter=event_time@1 < cutoff@0
    ProjectionExec: expr=[25 as cutoff]
      PlaceholderRowExec
    DataSourceExec: partitions=1, partition_sizes=[1]
```

The equivalent query:

```sql
EXPLAIN FORMAT INDENT
SELECT account_id, event_time, 25 AS cutoff
FROM events
WHERE event_time < 25;
```

produces:

```text
ProjectionExec: expr=[account_id@0 as account_id, event_time@1 as event_time, 25 as cutoff]
  FilterExec: event_time@1 < 25
    DataSourceExec: partitions=1, partition_sizes=[1]
```

Executing both queries returns the same rows: `('a', 10, 25)` and `('b', 20, 25)`. This small example demonstrates the plan rewrite opportunity; it does not measure the ordering or memory benefit.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Rewrite an inner join with a provably single constant row into:

1. A filter on the other input, with the constant-side column references replaced by literals.
2. A projection that restores the original output columns, including any constant-side columns still needed.

An initial physical optimization could recognize `ProjectionExec` of literals over `PlaceholderRowExec` on either side of `NestedLoopJoinExec`.

Please also cover constants introduced during physical optimization. `AggregateStatistics` can replace a scalar aggregate with exactly this constant projection/placeholder shape. A logical-only rewrite would miss that opportunity, so the physical rewrite should run after that folding and before distribution/ordering enforcement.

Correctness considerations:

- Prove there is exactly one row overall, including partitioning; an estimated row count of one is insufficient.
- Preserve SQL NULL behavior in the substituted predicate, output types/nullability, column positions, and embedded join projections.
- Start with literal expressions; do not change evaluation counts for volatile expressions or evaluate arbitrary subplans during optimization.
- Keep the initial scope to inner joins; outer/semi/anti joins need separate reasoning.

Suggested regression coverage includes the constant input on either side, NULL literals, predicates that evaluate to false/NULL, retained/pruned constant columns, and a constant row produced by `AggregateStatistics`. An ordered, multi-partition input should also verify that valid ordering reaches downstream aggregation.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- Manually rewrite SQL to use a literal filter. This works for an explicitly known literal, but does not cover a bound that becomes constant only after statistics-based folding.
- Teach `NestedLoopJoinExec` to preserve order for a proven single-row input. This could help ordering, but still retains the join machinery and does not expose the literal predicate as a regular filter.

### Additional context

Relevant code:

- [AggregateStatistics creates the constant projection/placeholder subtree](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/e732212cabd030d500efc35049448b3714017c7b/datafusion/physical-optimizer/src/aggregate_statistics.rs).
- [EliminateJoin handles other join simplifications](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/e732212cabd030d500efc35049448b3714017c7b/datafusion/optimizer/src/eliminate_join.rs).
- [NestedLoopJoinExec declares neither input order preserved](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/e732212cabd030d500efc35049448b3714017c7b/datafusion/physical-plan/src/joins/nested_loop_join.rs#L453-L456).
